name: 25LC640AT-I_SN
title: 25AA640A/25LC640A: 64 Kbit SPI serial EEPROM
summary: A 64 Kbit (8192 x 8) electrically erasable PROM reached over an SPI-compatible serial bus with clock, data-in, data-out and chip-select lines, plus a hold input to pause a transfer and a write-protect input. The 25AA640A works from 1.8 V and the 25LC640A from 2.5 V, both up to 5.5 V, with a clock up to 10 MHz at 4.5 V and above. Writes go through a 32-byte page with a self-timed cycle of 5 ms max; a quarter, half or all of the array can be locked through STATUS register bits. 25LC640AT-I/SN is the 2.5 V device, industrial range, in the 3.90 mm SOIC on tape and reel.
key_figures: 10 MHz at 4.5-5.5 V; 5 MHz at 2.5-4.5 V; 3 MHz at 1.8-2.5 V

operation.text: The device is an SPI slave with an 8-bit instruction register. CS must be low and HOLD high for a whole operation. SI is sampled on rising SCK edges, starting with the first rising edge after CS falls, and SO changes after falling edges; the timing diagrams show SPI modes 0,0 and 1,1. Instructions, addresses and data travel most significant bit first. A microcontroller without an SPI port can drive the bus from general I/O lines in firmware.
Every read or write carries a 16-bit address after the instruction byte; the top three address bits are ignored, leaving 0000h to 1FFFh.

Pull CS low, send READ (03h) and the address; the byte at that address then shifts out on SO. Further clocks keep reading following bytes as the internal pointer steps up; past 1FFFh it wraps to 0000h, so a read can run on without limit. Raising CS ends the read.

No write to the array or STATUS register completes until WREN has armed the write enable latch. WREN (06h) sets it and WRDI (04h) clears it. CS must go high after the eight WREN bits to set the latch; a WRITE sent in the same CS-low period as WREN is not stored. The latch is cleared at power-up and after a successful WRDI, WRSR or WRITE.

With the latch set, pull CS low and send WRITE (02h), the address and from 1 to 32 data bytes, all inside one 32-byte page. CS must rise right after bit D0 of the last byte for the write to start; raising it at any other point aborts the write. The STATUS register (WPEN, WIP, WEL, BP1, BP0) can be read while the cycle runs, but the array cannot. The latch clears when the cycle ends.

Physical pages start at multiples of 32 and end at the next multiple minus one. A page write that runs past the end of its page wraps to the start of the same page and overwrites what was there rather than moving on to the next page; software has to keep each page write within one page.

RDSR (05h) returns the STATUS register at any time, including during a write cycle, and keeps returning it for as long as CS stays low. WIP shows a write in progress. WEL shows the latch and is read-only; WREN and WRDI change it whatever the write-protect state. BP1 and BP0 are nonvolatile and select the protected blocks.

WRSR (01h) followed by one data byte writes the nonvolatile STATUS bits: BP1 and BP0 lock none, the upper quarter, the upper half or all of the array, and WPEN arms the WP pin. Once a complete WRSR sequence has been clocked in, CS going high launches the internal write cycle.

Hardware protection is on with WPEN = 1 and the WP pin low, and off when WP is high or WPEN is 0. While on, only writes to the nonvolatile STATUS bits are blocked; everything else works normally. With WPEN = 1, holding WP low through a STATUS write sequence cancels it; WP falling after an internal write cycle has begun has no effect on it. With WPEN at 0 the pin is ignored, so the part can sit on a board with WP grounded and still have its STATUS register written.

Against stray writes: the latch is clear at power-up; WREN must be sent before each write; the latch clears after every byte, page or STATUS write; a write cycle starts only if CS rises after the right number of clocks; and array accesses during an internal write cycle are ignored while programming carries on.

After power is applied the part sits in standby, drawing little current, with CS high, the write enable latch is clear and SO is high impedance. CS must go from high to low before any operation can begin.
Raising CS during a programming cycle does not stop it; the device enters standby once the cycle finishes. Deselected, the device floats SO so several parts can share one SPI bus.

HOLD suspends a transfer in mid-sequence without having to resend it, for example so the host can serve other devices on a shared clock. The device must stay selected. HOLD has to fall with SCK low; if SCK is high the pause starts at the next high-to-low SCK transition; to resume, HOLD must rise while SCK is low. During the pause SI, SCK and SO are high impedance and edges on them are ignored, apart from CS. Taking HOLD low at any time floats SO. When HOLD is released the operation continues from where it stopped.
Rated for 1,000,000 erase/write cycles and data retention of more than 200 years, with ESD protection above 4000 V. The erase and write cycles are self-timed, 5 ms max.
